title: Instability in the US and Western Europe, 2010 to 2020
claim: The next decade would likely be a period of growing instability in the United States and Western Europe.
finding: Riots and anti-government demonstrations rose sharply after 2010 in the US, UK, France, Italy and Spain. In the US both rose roughly tenfold.
note: Checked by the forecaster and a co-author, using data to 2018. They note the data's known biases and that the countries are not independent cases.
claim_source: Turchin, Political instability may be a contributor in the coming decade, Nature 463, 608 (2010)

title: Which countries face instability within two years
claim: A model using a few variables, led by regime type, can tell countries heading for instability two years ahead.
who: Political Instability Task Force (Goldstone and others)
finding: Over 80% accuracy on instability onsets from 1955 to 2003, with 1995 to 2004 held back for testing.
later_check: An independent re-test found accuracy peaked in those held-back years and was relatively poor in later ones, and not only because of the Arab uprisings.
note: The re-testers conclude that the drivers of instability change over time.
claim_source: Goldstone and others, American Journal of Political Science (2010)
test_source: Goldstone and others, American Journal of Political Science (2010)
later_source: Bowlsby, Chenoweth, Hendrix and Moyer, British Journal of Political Science (2019)

title: The Limits to Growth scenarios
claim: If growth continued unchanged, food, industrial output and then population would decline within this century.
who: Meadows, Meadows, Randers and Behrens, a report for the Club of Rome
finding: Recent data sat close to all four scenarios tested. The two closest show growth stalling over the next decade; only one of them ends in collapse.
note: The scenarios only split apart after 2020, so the data cannot yet say which path the world is on. The test used scenarios from the model's later updates as well as the 1972 book.
claim_source: The Limits to Growth (1972), digital first edition, Dartmouth Library

title: Changes in conflict deaths in Africa, October 2020 to March 2021
claim: Statistical models can forecast where deaths from armed conflict will rise or fall over the coming months.
finding: Forecasts were locked in by September 2020 and scored on what then happened. Models beat a simple baseline, and a combination of all the teams' models beat the average single model.
note: Scored by a committee independent of the organisers and the teams. The forecast window was six months.
claim_source: Hegre, Vesco and Colaresi, International Interactions (2022)
later_source: Peace Research Institute Oslo, summary of the results

title: Warning signs before Pueblo societies transformed
claim: Societies lose resilience before they collapse or transform, and this shows up as a slowing recovery from small shocks.
who: Scheffer, van Nes, Bird, Bocinsky and Kohler, PNAS
finding: In tree-ring records of building activity from about AD 500 to 1300, the warning signal rose before four of five major transformations.
note: Found looking back at transitions already known. The authors say the signal can have other causes, and that their records are short.

title: Warning signs before Stone Age population crashes in Europe
claim: Early warning signals used in ecology can show when a human population is close to collapse.
finding: In radiocarbon dates from about 8,000 to 4,000 years ago, seven of nine European regions showed the warning signal before their population fell.
note: The collapse dates were picked by looking at the curves first, and the result is weaker without the authors' tuned statistic. They call it a first attempt.
claim_source: Downey, Haas and Shennan, PNAS (2016), author's copy
test_source: Downey, Haas and Shennan, PNAS (2016), author's copy
